question: A scheduler keeps delayed jobs in an array and, every 100 ms, runs `jobs.sort((a, b) => a.runAt - b.runAt)` and checks `jobs[0]`. With 200 000 scheduled jobs, CPU usage is high even when nothing is due. What is the better structure?
options: A min-heap by `runAt`: `peek` is O(1), and each insert or removal is O(log n)
A linked list sorted by insertion time
explanation: The scheduler only ever needs the earliest job. A heap keeps it at the root without re-sorting everything; durable schedulers do the same with a Redis sorted set or an indexed column.

question: Two jobs with the same priority are pushed into a binary heap: `A` first, then `B`. Which one is popped first?
options: Always `A`, heaps are FIFO among equals
Always `B`, heaps are LIFO among equals
Either one: heaps are not stable; add an increasing sequence number as a tie-breaker if FIFO matters
The heap throws because priorities must be unique
explanation: Sift operations move equal items around without regard to insertion order. A `(priority, sequence)` comparison restores FIFO among equals.

question: You need the 20 slowest requests from a log of 50 million lines streamed from storage. Which approach fits?
options: Load every line into an array and sort it
Stream the lines into a min-heap capped at 20 items: O(n log 20) time and constant memory
Use a max-heap containing all 50 million entries
explanation: A bounded min-heap holds the current top 20; its root is the weakest of them, so each new line is compared against it and the heap never grows past k.
